t: Install, check, connect, and fill a demo form in five minutes. Install Ostler, check that it can drive Chrome, connect your agent, and fill a demo form. About five minutes, most of it compiling. Note Status: v0.2, early. Ostler is tested against real Chrome and a real Qdrant server, but only on local fixtures, not the open web. A design review found real flaws and lists them openly with a fix order. Read what that means before relying on it.

You need Chrome or Chromium (Ostler drives a real browser) and Rust 1.89 or newer to build from source. cargo install --git https://github.com/inamdarmihir/ostler ostler Prebuilt binaries, npx and crates.io are described on the Install page. Nothing is published to crates.io or npm yet, so building from source is the path that works today.

When something is wrong it prints the fix. See Troubleshooting if it does not pass.

Rerun the same install command. install.sh replaces the binary in place. Then reconnect your MCP client (Claude Code: /mcp ; others: restart it) so it starts the new binary.

Delete the ostler binary ( ~/.local/bin/ostler , or ~/.cargo/bin/ostler ), and ~/.config/ostler and ~/.cache/ostler if you want the settings and the npx download gone. Memory lives in your Qdrant, not on disk here. ostler memory wipe --yes erases it, so run that first if you want it gone.

By default, nothing apart from the binary and, if you run ostler init , the config file ~/.config/ostler/config.toml (owner-only permissions). With sealed memory, a key file memory.key next to the config. Chrome uses a throwaway profile unless you pass --profile-dir . Ostler sends no telemetry.

install.sh is served from this site and verifies a checksum before installing; on a mismatch it installs nothing and runs nothing. It installs to ~/.local/bin by default ( OSTLER_INSTALL_DIR changes that, OSTLER_VERSION pins a version) and never edits your shell profile or your agent's config. You can read the script first: install.sh .

How keys become fields, how values are verified by read-back, and what submit results mean. Ostler's form engine is built so the model states intent once and the engine does the mechanics: it resolves each key to a field, fills in order, lets dependent controls appear, reads every value back, and reports what actually happened.

form_inspect returns typed fields: kind, label, required, options, pattern, current value, and any error. It also lists submit controls and says what memory knows about this form. form_fill takes {label | name | ref: value} for the whole form. form_submit clicks the submit or next control and reports the outcome. Dependent dropdowns, multi-step wizards, input masks, comboboxes, shadow DOM and same-origin iframes are handled inside these calls. See the tools reference for parameters.

s: How a key becomes a field
t: Keys are resolved in this order: exact ref, then name or id, then label, then fuzzy label. A key can match by ref, name, label or fuzzy label, and keys are resolved against every visible field once, so an ambiguous key cannot win by elimination. Ambiguity is reported, never guessed. If two fields match equally well, the report says ambiguous and asks for the ref. email finds "E-mail address", because a key equal to a run of the label's words written together matches, but two equally plausible fields are still refused. A key that matches nothing is UNMATCHED . It is not dropped silently, and the fill report only counts as OK if no key was unmatched. Forms re-mounted by a framework are

s: How a key becomes a field
t: followed.

The engine converts the value for the field before writing it: you send field written "Germany" select the option index for that option text "March 5, 2001" date 2001-03-05 "3:30 PM" time 15:30 03/04/2024 date refused as ambiguous (day-first or month-first), so the agent must say which Fields are filled in document order and the form is re-inspected after every field , so a dependent control (State after Country) appears before it is needed.

After writing a field, the engine reads the value back from the live page and compares it by field type. A value the page rewrote or cleared fails. A datetime-local must read back as the requested instant. A combobox must show the option you asked for. A longer option that merely contains it is a mismatch ("United States" versus "United States Minor Outlying Islands"), and the in-page picker only picks an exact, normalised option label, listing the options otherwise. Values the page legitimately reformats, such as (555) 123-4567 , are reported as reformatted , not as errors. Only exact matches and genuine reformatting pass. form_fill reports unsettled (a count) when the page was still busy

at the end of the fill, so the verdicts can be treated with care. Typed input is tried first, because it fires the same events a user would. If the page rejects it (masked or framework-controlled inputs), the engine retries with the native value setter plus events. Fills also send one harmless keyup , because some date pickers learn the text only from that event.

Just before clicking submit, form_submit re-reads the fields it verified and reports any the page cleared or rewrote in between as CHANGED BEFORE SUBMIT . This was added after a date picker was reported verified and then submitted empty.

result meaning Submitted the page accepted it: a new URL, or new confirmation text appeared after the click (for example a form that posts in the background and says "Thanks!" in place) Advanced the page moved to the next step of a wizard; repeat inspect, fill, submit NOT ACCEPTED the page reported problems, and the page's own messages follow SERVER ERROR the site answered the submit with an HTTP error (4xx/5xx) and showed no validation messages. The data may or may not have been stored: do not report it as submitted and do not retry blindly; check with snapshot or ask the user Nothing changed the form stayed put and said nothing visible. Check with snapshot ; do not resubmit blindly,

because it may have gone through With several forms on a page, form_submit with no form or control submits the form form_fill last filled; if none was filled it refuses and lists the forms rather than guessing the first. A thank-you page that still has an optional input (a newsletter box, a search) counts as Submitted , not Advanced , unless something on it is required, it has a step counter, or it has a "next" button.

Fields marked invalid only by colour (a red border, outline or glow, or red message text with no ARIA or class) and floating toasts or banners are reported as field and page errors. An error that was already on a field before the fill is flagged as possibly stale. An error message belongs to the field it follows, not to every field sharing a wrapper, and Bootstrap 3 .help-block is help text unless the group is .has-error .

Only real action buttons are submit candidates. The header's "Search" button, anything inside header , nav or role=search , and type-less buttons whose label says nothing about submitting ("Show tips") do not count.

Calendar date pickers on read-only inputs are handled heuristically: when a text field is read-only and the value is a date, the engine opens the popup, navigates months and clicks the day. It fails with a reason, not silently, when no popup or navigation is found. The heuristic looks for a month header, previous and next controls and day cells. Dropdown-only and year-only pickers are not handled.

Two tools help when a form is not obvious: look returns a screenshot with every clickable element boxed and numbered, and a legend such as e6 button "Send" -> submits the form . snapshot with a heading's ref reads just that section. A CAPTCHA, hCaptcha, Turnstile or "verify you are human" wall is reported with a CHALLENGE: line at the top of the result. The agent should stop retrying and ask you; with --headed , wait_for_human waits while you complete it. Ostler never solves or bypasses these ( ADR-0009 ).

Cross-origin iframes and closed shadow roots are invisible to the injected runtime. 2FA, CAPTCHA solving and anti-bot evasion are out of scope. Fill on very large forms (thousands of fields) is slow, because every key re-reads the form. It has been evaluated on local fixtures, not on the open web. See Benchmarks .
The reasoning, with the alternatives that were rejected, is in ADR-0004 (injected runtime) and ADR-0005 (form model and verification). A summary is on the Architecture page.

What is stored, what sealing hides and does not, local embeddings, per-tenant tokens. Memory is optional. Browsing and form filling need no account and no key. When you turn it on, Ostler saves facts you told it, which fact fills which field on which site, and what went wrong on a form, in your own Qdrant . This page is exact about what is stored, what is encrypted, and what is not hidden. The sealing, local-embedding and per-tenant-token features below are described in the changelog's Unreleased section: they are on main and not in a tagged release yet. Unreleased

Three Qdrant collections, multi-tenant through a tenant payload index: collection holds never holds ostler_profile facts you saved ( email , company , …) passwords, card numbers, anything that looks sensitive ostler_playbooks per site and form: which fact fills which field, with wins, losses and last verified time the values themselves ostler_episodes what went wrong on a form, so it is not repeated secrets Ostler sends no telemetry. Disk holds nothing by default, apart from a Chrome profile if you pass --profile-dir , and the config and key files described below. Secrets are refused by the memory API (password, token and card-like keys, and card-number-like values), sensitive fields are

never auto-filled from memory nor stored by --learn , and sensitive values are masked in tool output. Detection is heuristic (names, autocomplete tokens, digit patterns): a secret stored under an innocuous key with an innocuous value will not be caught. Learned values never overwrite facts you saved. --learn is off by default. Ostler records how forms were filled automatically (structure only), but stores your data only when you opt in with --learn or call memory_remember .

s: Sealing: encrypt before it reaches Qdrant
t: With memory in Qdrant, payloads are sealed on your machine by default ( --seal auto ). Unreleased Fact values, descriptions, playbooks and episodes are encrypted with AES-256-GCM , with the point id bound in as associated data. Site names, field labels, profile keys and fingerprints are replaced by keyed hashes (HMAC-SHA-256) , and point ids are keyed too, so filters still work but the server cannot test guesses ("passport number") against what it stores. Episodes are redacted before they are embedded or stored: emails, runs of four or more digits (phones, PIN codes, card numbers) and URL query strings are masked, in addition to the values the agent typed. The key lives in OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY

s: Sealing: encrypt before it reaches Qdrant
t: or an owner-only memory.key next to the config file, created atomically on first use. Back it up: there is no recovery. If you lose it, sealed memory is unreadable. --seal on forces it; --seal off opts out (and ostler doctor and serve warn that anyone who can read your Qdrant can then read your saved facts and the sites you use).

s: What is hidden, and what is not
t: someone who can read your Qdrant (operator, leaked key, backup) sees Fact values and descriptions encrypted Playbooks and episodes (contents) encrypted; episodes are also redacted of emails and numbers Site names, field labels, profile keys, fingerprints keyed hashes only The vector visible. With --embeddings cloud , the field text is sent to Qdrant Cloud Inference to be embedded, and vectors of labels reveal roughly what they say. Use --embeddings ollama to keep text local Tenant name visible Win and loss counters, timing, point counts visible The key is, in order of precedence, the OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY variable, or the store chosen by key_store ( OSTLER_KEY_STORE ): file (default, owner-only

s: What is hidden, and what is not
t: memory.key ) or keychain (macOS Keychain / Linux Secret Service). Unreleased ostler memory key export --yes-print and ostler memory key import back it up and restore it.

Memory saved before sealing was on is invisible until you run: ostler config set seal on ostler memory seal Saved facts are copied into sealed form and read back to check them before the old plaintext points are deleted, so it is safe to interrupt and run again. Learned skills and episodes from that time are dropped and relearned.

By default Ostler embeds text with Qdrant Cloud Inference ( sentence-transformers/all-minilm-l6-v2 , 384 dimensions). To keep the text on your machine, embed locally with Ollama: Unreleased ostler serve --embeddings ollama --embedding-model <model> --embedding-dim <dims> --embeddings where text is embedded notes cloud (default) inside Qdrant Cloud Inference needs Inference enabled on the cluster. Field text is sent to Qdrant. Covered by request-shape tests; not run against a live Cloud cluster by the maintainers ollama on your machine, through an Ollama server only vectors reach Qdrant. --embedding-url defaults to http://127.0.0.1:11434 ( OSTLER_EMBEDDING_URL ); set --embedding-model and

--embedding-dim to match the model. Remote plain- http embedders are refused dev-hash on your machine, deterministic hash not semantic. Exact-key and autocomplete lookups work; fuzzy meaning does not. For open-source Qdrant development Exact signals need no vectors: lookups by playbook mapping and autocomplete token use payload filters.

Plain http:// to a non-loopback Qdrant is refused , because the API key and facts would cross the network unencrypted. --allow-insecure-qdrant ( OSTLER_ALLOW_INSECURE_QDRANT ) overrides it for links already protected by a VPN or tunnel. Unreleased If Qdrant fails twice in a row (transport error or 5xx), lookups are skipped for 30 seconds and tool results start with Note: memory is unavailable (...); continuing without it. Requests time out after 4 seconds.

By default all tenants share three collections, separated by a tenant filter in every query. A leaked admin key exposes every tenant in that mode. For stronger separation: Unreleased --isolation collection gives each tenant its own collections. ostler memory token mints a JWT that Qdrant itself limits to those collections, read-write or --read-only , and expiring. A leaked client token then exposes one tenant, not the cluster. Qdrant must run with service.jwt_rbac: true , and an admin must create the collections first. # 1. as admin: create alice's collections (`ostler memory list` does it) export QDRANT_URL=https://<cluster>.cloud.qdrant.io:6333 QDRANT_API_KEY=<admin key> export

OSTLER_ISOLATION=collection OSTLER_TENANT=alice ostler memory list # 2. mint a token for alice (30 days by default; add --read-only for search-only) ostler memory token --days 30 # 3. give alice the token instead of the admin key # QDRANT_API_KEY=<token> with --isolation collection --tenant alice Tested on a real Qdrant 1.20: another tenant's collections answer 403, and expired, forged and read-only tokens are refused. Qdrant 1.20 rejects the older per-point payload claim as deprecated, so isolation is per collection . Not covered: the default shared isolation shares collections, so a leaked admin key exposes every tenant, and collection isolation needs jwt_rbac and an admin who creates the
collections. Over A2A , all conversations share one tenant; run one server per tenant if callers must not see each other's profile.

For a field, in order of reliability: the form's own playbook mapping; an exact autocomplete -token match against your facts (payload filter, no vectors); a playbook from a similar form on the same site (a redesign or sibling form); semantic vector search. form_fill with auto: "required" fills what memory can supply and reports the rest. Semantic matches need a margin over the runner-up and never apply to labels about other people. Playbooks persist only exact (playbook or autocomplete ) matches.

Ostler needs no model to judge whether a fill worked: the browser reads every value back and the page accepts or rejects the submit, so every outcome is ground truth. step what happens Qdrant feature recall exact form first; after a redesign, mappings transfer from a similar form on the same site with the same label keyword-array filter on labels_norm and host , tenant index rank proven, recently verified skills beat stale or failing ones Query API prefetch and a score-boosting formula (similarity, smoothed win rate and exp_decay on verified_ts ) reinforce verified fields on accepted submits add wins per mapping integer payload indexes demote a mapping that loses more than it wins is dropped

forget ostler memory prune --days 90 removes stale, unproven skills; serve also forgets those not verified for 180 days on start ( --retain-days , 0 keeps them). Saved facts never expire range filter on verified_ts On a scripted site with redesigned forms, correct suggestions went from 1 to 8 of 10 fillable fields, with zero wrong fills in both conditions. That is a synthetic fixture, not real sites ( ADR-0008 ).

Config file, environment variables, every serve and a2a flag. Settings come from, in order: command-line flag, then environment variable, then the config file, then the default. One path per setting, so what ostler serve does is what ostler doctor tested.

ostler init Asks for a Qdrant URL and API key (skip both for no memory), a tenant name, and whether to enable --learn and --lean . It writes the config file with owner-only permissions and immediately tests the connection. Non-interactively: ostler init --qdrant-url https://<cluster>.cloud.qdrant.io --qdrant-api-key "$KEY" --tenant alice The :6333 port is added to Qdrant Cloud URLs for you. If the connection test fails the settings are still saved, so you can fix one value instead of retyping everything: ostler config show # key is masked ostler config set qdrant_url http://localhost:6333 ostler config unset learn ostler config path # ~/.config/ostler/config.toml

The threat model: what Ostler does, and what it does not do. This page is the repository's SECURITY.md . For how the memory-related rows work in practice, see Memory and privacy . Ostler lets an AI agent drive a real browser and stores some user data. Treat it like any tool that can act on your behalf.

Please use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting for this repository ("Security" tab → "Report a vulnerability"). Do not open a public issue for something exploitable. There is no bounty. This is a pre-1.0 project maintained by individuals; we will acknowledge reports as quickly as we can.

threat what we do what we do not do Prompt injection from a web page Page-derived text is wrapped in <page_content untrusted="true"> : page content, but also titles, URLs, dialog text and the look legend, which used to sit on trusted lines. Text a person cannot see (opacity 0, zero font size, far off-screen, same colour as the background) is left out and counted, so a hidden instruction never reaches the model. Server instructions tell the model not to follow page text. We cannot stop a model from being persuaded by text a person can also see. Hidden-text detection judges colour only against a solid background; gradients, images and clip -style screen-reader text are not treated as hidden.

Use --allow-domain and --require-confirm-submit for anything sensitive. Agent navigates somewhere it should not Domain allowlist enforced inside the browser. Every request the page makes is held and checked whatever its type (documents, images, stylesheets, scripts, fetch /XHR, beacons, event streams), and Chrome is started with a resolver rule that makes every other host unresolvable, which also covers WebSockets and the first request of a popup. Entries may pin a port ( example.com:8443 ). Only http(s); file: needs --allow-file . Tested with a canary server on a non-allowlisted origin: no request arrives through , a stylesheet, fetch , XHR, a beacon, a WebSocket, EventSource , a form

POST, a redirect, a meta refresh, a script navigation or window.open , by hostname or by IP literal. With no allowlist, --block-private-networks refuses loopback, private, link-local (cloud metadata), CGNAT and internal-looking hosts, and names that resolve to them. Independently of that flag, navigating to a literal link-local address (169.254.0.0/16 including 169.254.169.254, fe80::/10 , fd00:ec2::254 ) or a well-known metadata hostname ( metadata.google.internal ) is refused unless you allowlist it. An entry without a port allows every port on that host. Ports are checked on the requests interception sees; the browser-wide resolver rule works on hosts only, so treat a port pin as defence

in depth, not isolation, for WebSockets. The private-network check resolves a name before Chrome does, so a DNS-rebinding server can answer differently the second time: use an allowlist where that matters. --block-private-networks is off by default for serve because coding agents browse local dev servers (and the demo fixtures live on loopback); it is on by default for a2a . The always-on metadata check covers navigations and literal addresses only: without an allowlist, a page's own sub-requests and names that merely resolve to a metadata address are not checked. Not a sandbox against a compromised browser. Irreversible submissions --require-confirm-submit blocks every non-GET request

unless it happens inside form_submit with confirm=true . Off by default. A GET with side effects, and WebSockets, are not covered. The first request of a popup window and requests from cross-site iframes (their own browser processes) are covered too: Chrome is told to hold such targets at start ( Target.setAutoAttach with waitForDebuggerOnStart ) and interception is switched on before they are released, so --allow-domain host:port pins and the gate apply to them (tested with a canary: popup POST, popup GET to another port, cross-site iframe POST/ fetch /image). A submit that is cancelled mid-flight now closes the gate again. At most 8 popups are adopted (the rest are closed before they run).

A popup opened by the form you confirmed inherits the confirmation for its first request only, so a hostile page that opens a window during a confirmed submit can let that popup's first request through. File exfiltration through an upload field File fields are refused unless you pass --upload-dir DIR . A path is resolved first ( .. and symlinks included) and must land inside an allowed directory; the browser is handed the resolved path. Anything inside an allowed directory can be attached to any page the agent visits, so keep it small and free of secrets. A page's own "are you sure?" dialog confirm() and prompt() are dismissed, so a site's "Delete everything?" is not confirmed by a browser

nobody is watching, and the agent is told what happened. alert() and beforeunload are acknowledged. --accept-dialogs restores auto-accept for sites that need it. A dismissed confirm can leave a flow stuck; the agent sees the dialog text and can ask you. A remote agent over A2A Loopback by default; bearer token required to listen elsewhere; Origin and Host checks against browser-based attacks; per-conversation browsers; submit needs an explicit confirm; private and internal addresses are refused unless you pass --allow-private-networks . No TLS (use a reverse proxy). All conversations share one memory tenant. Always pass --allow-domain . See docs/A2A.md . Secrets in memory The memory API

refuses password/token/card-like keys and card-number-like values; sensitive fields are never auto-filled from memory nor stored by --learn ; sensitive values are masked in tool output; playbooks store structure only, never values. Detection is heuristic (names, autocomplete tokens, digit patterns). A secret stored under an innocuous key with an innocuous value will not be caught. Cross-user data exposure Every memory point carries a tenant ; every query filters on it; isolation is tested on a real Qdrant. With --isolation collection each tenant has its own collections and ostler memory token mints a JWT Qdrant itself limits to them (tested on Qdrant 1.20: other tenants answer 403). The

default shares collections, so a leaked admin key exposes every tenant. Collection isolation needs jwt_rbac and an admin who creates the collections. Someone who can read your Qdrant (operator, leaked key, backup) Payloads are sealed on your machine (AES-256-GCM); site names, labels, keys and point ids are keyed hashes; episodes are redacted of emails and numbers; plain http:// to a remote Qdrant is refused. The vector is not hidden: with --embeddings cloud the field text is sent to Qdrant Cloud Inference, and vectors of labels reveal roughly what they say. Use --embeddings ollama to keep text local. Tenant name, win/loss counters, timing and point counts stay visible. The key is a file or

env var by default (optionally the macOS Keychain or Linux Secret Service via key_store = keychain ; the Linux path is untested against a real keyring). Lose it and sealed memory is unreadable; serve refuses to start rather than silently replace a key that cannot open existing memory. Malicious page attacking the runtime The injected runtime avoids eval and never executes page-supplied strings; it works on DOM objects. The runtime shares a JS world with the page, so a hostile page could tamper with it (e.g. to mislead reads). Do not rely on it for adversarial pages. Local exposure Chrome is launched with a throwaway profile and talks to Ostler over a pipe ( --remote-debugging-pipe ). There

is no debugging port, so no other local user can connect to the browser, and Chrome exits by itself if Ostler dies. Tested: no listening socket in the browser's process tree (the WebSocket mode shows one). OSTLER_CDP_TRANSPORT=ws brings back the old unauthenticated localhost port, for debugging only. With --profile-dir your logged-in sessions live on disk, readable by your own account and by any process running as you. Not audited. No security review has been done by a third party.

outside the allowlist and loads a page that tries to reach it through an image, a stylesheet, fetch , XHR, a beacon, a WebSocket, EventSource , a form POST, a redirect, a meta refresh, a script navigation and window.open . A control run with no allowlist must reach the canary, so "nothing arrived" cannot be a broken test. The allowlist, screenshot and trust-boundary ( page_text_never_reaches_a_trusted_line ) tests were run against the code before their fixes and failed there. The upload, dialog, port, private-network and debugging-port tests pair each protection with its opt-out or a control run, so they cannot pass by testing nothing.

Qdrant (your cluster): facts you saved, form playbooks (field labels and which fact filled them), episodes (error messages from forms), all tagged with your tenant. By default these are encrypted before upload ( --seal ); the key is memory.key beside your config file or OSTLER_MEMORY_KEY . Let other agents hand Ostler forms over Agent2Agent v1.0. Ostler can be driven by another agent over A2A (v1.0, JSON-RPC over HTTP, SSE streaming), as well as by a coding agent over MCP. Use MCP when one agent owns the browser; use A2A when another agent (or service) should be able to hand Ostler a form as a task. ostler a2a --allow-domain example.com # http://127.0.0.1:8765 curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/.well-known/agent-card.json Ostler is a tool, not a language model . It understands structured requests, not free text. It tells a client so (it answers chatter with a message that shows the expected shape).

Send SendMessage (or SendStreamingMessage ) with a data part: { "url" : "https://example.com/signup" , "values" : { "Email" : "ada@example.com" , "Country" : "Germany" }, "submit" : true} field meaning url page to open first. Omit to continue on the conversation's current page values {label | name | ref: value} , filled and verified by reading each field back auto required or all : fill the rest from the owner's saved profile (needs Qdrant memory) submit submit once everything is filled and verified confirm the caller agrees to the submission No values , no auto , no submit : it just inspects the form. A bare URL in a text part does the same.

state when what the client does TASK_STATE_COMPLETED inspected, filled, or submitted and accepted read the artifacts TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED required fields missing, a key matched nothing or was ambiguous, the page rejected a value, a wizard advanced, or it is waiting for {"confirm": true} reply on the same taskId with more values or confirm TASK_STATE_FAILED blocked by policy, timed out, or the page never accepted the submit read the result artifact TASK_STATE_CANCELED CancelTask Nothing is submitted until the caller says confirm: true , unless the server runs with --a2a-auto-submit . A remote agent can of course just send it; the point is that a human-in-the-loop client has a place to

stop. Each task has two artifacts: result (compact text) and data (the same information as JSON: missing , unmatched , fieldErrors , …). Both are marked metadata.untrusted: true because they contain text from the website. Treat them as data, never as instructions.

One A2A contextId is one Ostler session: its own Chrome, its own tabs , and its own shared context notes. Messages with the same contextId (or the same taskId ) continue where the last one stopped, e.g. the form that was filled is still open when {"confirm": true} arrives. Different contextId s can never see each other's pages. Each conversation is a Chrome process (about 400-650 MiB), so it is capped: --max-contexts (default 4), idle ones are closed after --idle-secs (default 300).

SendMessage , SendStreamingMessage , GetTask , ListTasks , CancelTask , SubscribeToTask . GetExtendedAgentCard and the push-notification methods return the A2A errors for "not supported" ( -32007 , -32003 ). Errors use the A2A codes ( -32001 task not found, -32002 not cancelable, -32004 unsupported operation, -32009 version not supported) with a google.rpc.ErrorInfo detail. A2A-Version must be 1.x if sent. A missing header is accepted (the spec says to assume 0.3, which this server does not implement, so being lenient here is a deliberate choice).

An A2A endpoint lets a network client steer a browser that can log in to things. Defaults are conservative: Binds 127.0.0.1 . Binding anything else requires --a2a-token (or OSTLER_A2A_TOKEN ); the server refuses to start otherwise. With a token, the RPC endpoint needs Authorization: Bearer … (compared in constant time). The Agent Card stays public, as the protocol expects, and advertises the scheme but never the token. Requests carrying an Origin header (a web page in a browser) are refused, and the Host header must be a loopback name or one you list with --allowed-host / --public-url . This blocks drive-by and DNS-rebinding attacks from a page open on the same machine. Always set

--allow-domain . Without it, any remote agent can send this browser to any public website. The allowlist is enforced inside the browser for every conversation (every request type, WebSockets included). Without an allowlist the server blocks loopback, private and cloud-metadata addresses so a remote agent cannot probe this machine's network ( --allow-private-networks turns that off); the server warns at startup. Uploads are refused unless you pass --upload-dir . TLS is not terminated here. Put it behind a reverse proxy for anything beyond localhost, and set --public-url . All conversations share one Qdrant tenant . If different callers must not see each other's saved profile, run one server
per tenant.

The official A2A Python SDK ( a2a-sdk 1.3.0) resolved the card, selected the JSON-RPC interface, streamed a three-turn conversation (input-required, input-required, completed) and received artifacts on every turn against the real binary. That was a manual check; the repository's own tests ( crates/ostler-a2a/tests ) use plain HTTP. Not implemented: gRPC and REST bindings, push notifications, extended cards, signed cards, and the v0.3 wire format.

t: Each has an ADR in docs/adr/ where the alternatives are written down. An injected runtime instead of CDP's accessibility tree. A single script ( runtime.js ) runs inside every document and does traversal, snapshotting and field manipulation. The cost: it is our code running in a hostile page's world, so it is written defensively (no eval , no page-supplied selectors executed as code) and it cannot see closed shadow roots or cross-origin frames. Unit costs, scaling limits, the moat question and what could go wrong. Written as the questions a skeptical investor or senior engineer would ask, answered with what we measured ( BENCHMARKS.md ) and clearly separated from what we assume. Where we do not know, we say so.

s: 2. Is the saving real, or an artefact of the baseline?
t: Partly baseline. The "per-field" comparison models the worst-case pattern (one call per field, full snapshot after each). Tools with batched fills close part of the gap. What stays differentiated even against a batched filler: verification by read-back, dependent dropdown/wizard handling in one call, shadow DOM/iframes, validation-error reporting, and cross-session memory. We do not yet have a head-to-head against other products on the same tasks; that is on the roadmap and we will publish it either way.

Per node (measured, 8-core laptop): 8 parallel sessions gave 354-393 tasks/min, p95 under 1 s, 100% success, flat latency, 450-550 MiB per session. Derived planning numbers, assuming CPU-bound at 0.5 CPU-s per task: ~7,000 tasks per core-hour; memory-bound at ~0.5 GiB per session: ~14 concurrent sessions per 8 GB, ~120 per 64 GB. Assumptions: Linux numbers will differ; real sites are heavier than fixtures (more CPU, more RAM per page); idle sessions hold memory. Treat as a first-order estimate until the Linux benchmark job reports. Memory layer (measured on real Qdrant): retrieval latency stays ~0.4 ms p50 from 20k to 200k points because queries are tenant-scoped via a payload index.

Throughput ~2.4-2.9k QPS with 16 clients on one laptop-hosted node. What does not scale yet (be skeptical here): Qdrant RAM per user is the open number. We saw ~6.8-8.4 KB per point at 200k points untuned, i.e. ~130-160 KB per user at 20 facts. At 1M users that is ~130-160 GB untuned. It is a loaded-and-queried figure, not isolated steady state, so it is an upper-ish bound, but it needs a proper sizing study with quantization and on-disk vectors before any capacity claim. Hosted multi-tenant browsers (isolation, anti-abuse, residential proxies, CAPTCHAs) are not built and are where hosted-browser companies spend most of their cost.

s: 4. What are the unit economics of a business around this?
t: This repository is an open-source tool (Apache-2.0), not a business. The plausible shapes, with their honest weaknesses: Pull-through for Qdrant Cloud. Each active user holds a small memory footprint and issues a few queries per form. Value to Qdrant is adoption and a reference workload, not direct revenue per user (the volume per user is small). Weakness: low revenue per seat. Hosted sessions (managed browsers with memory). Compute is cheap (section 1), so gross margin is high before proxies, CAPTCHAs and abuse handling, which is where margin disappears. Weakness: crowded, and the hard costs are the ones we have not built. Enterprise (audit log, policy, SSO, approval workflows, on-prem).

s: 4. What are the unit economics of a business around this?
t: Weakness: needs real-site reliability evidence first. We do not put revenue numbers here because we have no basis for them.

Honest answer: not the language, not the browser. agent-browser (Vercel) is already a native Rust CLI with MCP and ~45k stars; Rust is table stakes. What can compound: Per-user memory (playbooks, profile, known issues) is switching cost and quality that improves with use. A form corpus : fingerprints of forms and which strategies worked. Opt-in, anonymised cross-user sharing is a possible network effect, and a privacy risk that must be designed in from the start (not built). Published, reproducible benchmarks that others have to match. What can erode it: competitors adding memory (it is not hard in principle), and model vendors shipping first-party browser agents that need no external tool.

What changed, including the Unreleased section. Entries under Unreleased are on the main branch and are not in a tagged release yet. This includes sealed memory, local embeddings and per-tenant tokens; see Memory and privacy .

Popup and target hardening (second review). A page can no longer flood the browser with popups: at most 8 are adopted at once (held popups over the cap are closed before they can run, with one note), closed tabs are reaped, and the original page keeps answering (150 window.open calls used to produce 151 tabs and ~12 s of lag). A worker, service worker or iframe whose interception cannot be set up now stays paused and is closed instead of being resumed uninstrumented. The CDP event channel is 16x larger and a receiver that falls behind is told so: the popup watcher re-syncs against Target.getTargets and closes any page it does not know, and page/frame loops report the loss as a warning on the

next action. A confirmed form_submit whose form targets a new window ( target=_blank ) now goes through, while an unconfirmed one is still blocked (the popup inherits the opener's armed state for its first request only). Limits: a dropped Target.attachedToTarget for an iframe or worker, and a dropped Fetch.requestPaused , cannot be recovered (the request or frame stays paused: safe but stuck); more than 8 legitimate simultaneous popups are closed; a hostile page that opens a window during a confirmed submit can let that popup's first request through. A real Chrome buffer overflow was not reproduced. Second review round on the fill engine. (1) The faster settle (below) could report Verified

before a slow server-side check finished and the page then showed an error ("Username already taken", a rejected value in the fifth of five inputs that each fire the same validation request). Background classification no longer ages a request into the background by duration; recurrence only counts when no input happened in between (any input, change, click or keydown resets it); timers up to 2.5 s are waited for; the per-field wait ceiling is 3 s. Cost: a form whose every field triggers a ~1.5 s server check now takes that long per field, which is the honest price of reporting the late error. (2) A checkbox with its label before it no longer takes the label that belongs to the next control (

Email [x] Phone [x] ticked Email for "Phone"): the layout convention of the whole group decides, and an undecidable layout falls back to the field name instead of guessing. (3) A successful search no longer reads NOT ACCEPTED because a result snippet contains "invalid certificate error": plain-text error words count only when the page stayed on the same path and the text sits next to the form, not in a list or article. (4) Option labels like "Email" under a "Contact preference" radio group no longer make a real "Email" field ambiguous, and "billing address" / "shipping address" resolve through their fieldsets. (5) A read-only dd/mm/yyyy datepicker no longer fails after the date rewrite;

years outside 1900-2100 are refused and two-digit years expanded (a negative year used to be able to panic); an assumed mm/dd/yyyy is disclosed in the warning; a reordered radio/option group is re-resolved by label at fill time instead of by stale index; last_form no longer survives a navigation. (6) Page-controlled validation text could contain a newline and forge a trusted Ready: hint line in tool output; every page-derived note, warning and reason is now flattened to one bounded line. out readable ones; prune , probe_key and the legacy count read every point instead of the first 10,000; a value that JSON cannot round-trip exactly is refused instead of stored one digit off; the circuit breaker lets exactly one trial through after the cooldown; error text reaching the agent is capped, single-line and free of credentials (also for a local embedder URL); card numbers are caught through any separators and inside nested values; keychain tools time out after 20 s instead of hanging startup. 42 unit tests, 25 sealing fuzz tests, 10 redaction fuzz tests and 10 real-Qdrant hardening tests cover this.
